speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take your two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thankfully, we have effective, professional and responsive uniformed teams working to keep us safe – the Singapore Police Force (SPF), the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF), the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and the Internal Security Department (ISD).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But terrorism is not a fight they are to battle against alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is a prized jewel because of what Singaporeans stand for – meritocracy, diligence, multiracialism, unity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because of these attributes, many evil doers seek to do us harm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But should a terrorist threat ever vest on our shores, it is those very attributes that will enable us to overcome the disunity terrorism seeks to sow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Each Singaporean has a social role to provide a united multiracial response in the aftermath of a terror attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That duty cannot be left to the Home Team alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That way, our precious Singaporean unity, so unique to the world, will be preserved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are two reasons why the role of each Singaporean is particularly important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How Singaporeans react in the midst of a terror attack is very important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Relationships and mutual trust and understanding which undergird multiracialism are not something that can be manufactured or imposed top-down.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another example is a community-based women's group in Bangladesh which equips women to promote social cohesion and battle violent extremism in their roles as mothers, wives, sisters and daughters who shape the values of those in their family and community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as such exercises are being rolled out to prepare Singaporeans for a terror attack, it is important for every Singaporean to participate and play their important role in keeping Singapore safe when a terror attack vest on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can MHA foster such a relationship with Singaporeans to achieve that goal of a strong Singapore in the face of a terror attack?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Self-radicalisation through the Internet is also a threat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Indonesia, in the past, a method of recruitment was through online games.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the terrorist recruitment video in September 2017 featuring the Singaporean Abu Iqayl was analysed as a stepped-up attempt to reach out to a younger and better-educated audience in a predominately Malay/Muslim region.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our unique social fabric in Singapore, especially our multiracial way of life, is harmed by plans for, thoughts of, and actions towards violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Terrorism is an affront to all our communities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is an affront to the Chinese community; it is an affront to the Malay community; it is an affront to the Indian community; it is an affront to the Eurasian community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, how can we bolster our laws to prevent the spread of radicalised teachings that promote violent extremism?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Accompanying this is also a sense that certain religious practices and identities have become more exclusivist over time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The business owner, in his business calculations, had expected a healthy demand for such services.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This exclusivist arrangement could lead to reduced contact with other communities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is of concern to us because it is happening right next door across the Causeway.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Here in Singapore, we champion racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want to focus on the commonalities, not the differences amongst us.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Wherever possible, we want to enlarge the common spaces shared among different communities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is how we manifest our shared values, build our shared experiences and achieve our collective goals as a united nation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, we have to acknowledge that, as an open society, we are not immune to external influences.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we are not vigilant, what has happened elsewhere in the world could well happen to us.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Exclusivist and discriminatory practices along religious lines would splinter our society as we are one of the most religiously diverse countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry share with us an update on the measures to counter the threat of radicalisation?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we counter threats of segregationist teachings on the Internet, particularly social media?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is the Home Team progressing in its work with different religious and community groups to combat segregationist teachings in order to help preserve the religious harmony we all cherish today?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is unsettling to see acts of terror still happening all over the world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Although the incidents have happened in other countries, Singaporeans are acutely aware that the same tragedy can happen on our soil.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is worrying when we also hear reports of the arrests and detention of radicalised Singaporeans who could have potentially caused harm at home.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Ministry to give an update on the current level of threat.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is the current level of threat of terrorism on the international, regional and domestic fronts?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I trust the Ministry and the Home Team are taking all efforts to ensure that our country is prepared to deflect and respond to any potential attacks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe it would be good to assure Singaporeans of the counterterrorism efforts in place to protect Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on what has been done to build the Home Team's capabilities?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Aside from the Home Team, it is important that the community stays vigilant and is also equipped with the necessary preparedness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To this end, SGSecure has been an excellent effort in creating awareness and building the skills of members of the community in response to a terror attack.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are there means to measure the level of awareness and preparedness of the community?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What more can be done to equip our community with the necessary skills and protect them against any attacks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, loan sharks have been turning to online harassment of debtors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The aim of online harassment is the same as the offline mode, to shame the debtor in his community and harass the debtor's associates until he pays up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is one difference – the loan sharks are innovating to avoid detection and identification, for example, by stealing the debtor's identity and posting it, to utterly destroy his reputation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister also elaborate how the Police is combatting online forms of loan shark harassment so as to assure the public?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government's long-standing position has been that it does not officially reveal the countries from where these new citizens originate on the grounds of sensitivity of the country of origin of our new citizens and the implications and sensitivities for specific groups of persons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, in a similar reply to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) in 2016, the Government did not give any percentages but to say that the majority came from Southeast Asian countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry please elaborate on what sensitivities the Government is concerned about, particularly since Singapore's need for immigration is publicly well-known, along with the Government's stated position of keeping the racial percentages as close to their current levels as far as possible?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry provide specific details on the number of successful applications for the same period for applicants who had a monthly income of less than $3,500, $3,000 and $2,500 and confirm if there has been any change to the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority's (ICA's) evaluation criteria from 2016?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The details would provide some degree of certainty for foreign spouses married to Singaporeans when they apply for PR.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, can the Government share how many foreigners who are married to Singapore Citizens do not meet the Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) or LTVP-Plus (LTVP+) criteria but are granted short-term visit passes instead?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What are the main reasons for the rejection of their LTVP or LTVP+ applications, and what criteria does the Government use to reassess or review such applications?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2017, there appeared to be a number of vulnerable Singaporeans who were victims of abuse and the culprits managed to escape with relatively light sentences.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Notable instances include the intellectually disabled Annie Ee who was tortured to death; and martial art instructor Joshua Robinson who was only jailed for four years after committing the offence of statutory rape.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The abuse of vulnerable adults, including the elderly, disabled and infirm, are a growing phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There was an announcement in 2014 to introduce a Vulnerable Adults Act, but there has been not much news thereafter.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Annie Ee and Robinson cases have caused much public outrage, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Minister on the progress of the Vulnerable Adults Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does MHA intend to enhance our current laws to better protect the vulnerable groups in the society?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In some other countries, these groups are protected by specific laws.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In New Zealand, for example, the Protection of Personal and Property Rights (3PR) Act allows vulnerable people, defined as those who are old, sick or mentally-impaired, to appoint one or more people to be their enduring power of attorney, if they feel that they will be at risk of ill-treatment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In New York, the state Senate in 2015 passed a sweeping package of 10 Bills to protect vulnerable senior citizens from predatory financial schemes, physical and emotional abuse.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is time to enhance the protection for the vulnerable groups, to better protect those who cannot speak and to fend for those who are weak.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, some feel that their experiences are not well-understood and encounter insensitivities as they seek justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This retraumatises and discourages them from coming forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry provide mandatory and recurrent capacity-building for members at all levels of the criminal justice system, including lawyers, law enforcement officers and healthcare staff, so that they can better deal with survivors in a gender-sensitive way?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the ongoing review on marital rape, is the Ministry looking at a complete removal of immunity or considering other positions?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The number of child abuse cases has been increasing over the last four years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is a harrowing experience to have to recount the abuse one has suffered at the hands of a superior.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The pain is felt even more acutely when the victim is a minor, a child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This may be exacerbated when the victim feels uncertain about whether he or she will need to see the perpetrator again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, within the judicial process, as well as at the stage of investigations, how can the victim be made to feel less distraught when having to provide evidence against the alleged perpetrator?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have said before in this House that the 2010 Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) amendments introducing community-based sentencing for these offenders are a milestone.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This enables us to directly address the root cause of their offending behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are laudable steps in the right direction and deserve our support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This evidences, indeed, what our Government has always been saying about a just and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It would have been easier to just segregate the mentally-challenged offenders and put them away.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead, a lot more effort and resources are being put in to help rehabilitate them and bring them back to society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One area which I would like to suggest that MHA consider further strengthening is the framework involving the administration of a conditional warning in lieu of prosecution for mentally-challenged offenders, especially youthful offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members would note, the community-based sentencing regime would not apply to these offenders as they have not been charged in Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The warning in lieu of prosecution route may be employed for offenders with mental issues who have committed offences not assessed to be on the serious end of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For first-time offenders, they may be given an outright warning in lieu of prosecution if they are first offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As each case is different, there could be flexibility in devising a bespoke system for each offender based on his or her background and the specifics of the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am currently dealing with one case in Bukit Batok where the offender is a 15-year-old boy who has autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He decided not to attend school and instead, frequents the gaming arcades to feed his gaming addiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was previously given a stern warning for the offence of possessing an offensive weapon.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A few months later, he committed another offence of trespass into a school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without intervention, the chances of him reoffending and being charged in Court is high.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are at least six stakeholders dealing with his case: his parents, the Police, his school teachers, a social worker from a Family Service Centre, psychiatrist and psychologist, and the Social Service Office (SSO).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would require the Police to be assisted by the professionals who will have to recommend the appropriate treatment for the boy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The framework may require the boy to report frequently to the Police, so that his activities can be checked.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may require the boy to go to school regularly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may require him not to frequent gaming arcades.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may require him to take his medication in accordance with what has been prescribed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may also require the parents of the boys to furnish a bond, if it is assessed that the parents are not likely to provide sufficient support for the programme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such a regime, in my respectful opinion, will provide him with the best chance of not reoffending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would mean that the Police have to be given resources or access to resources within the community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a need to coordinate with different stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There may be a need to identify a proper liaison body, such as the SSO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not easy to implement, but it is important not just for the sake of the mentally-challenged offender, but his family and the community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This has important implications for our next generation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Even though there may be shifting attitudes towards drugs, we must not cave in to what I call the defeatist narrative of the West, which promotes legalisation for recreational drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There is nothing recreational about seeing whole families suffer physical, economic and mental harm across generations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) must continue to criminalise both the demand and supply elements of the drug transaction, that is, trafficking the drug, the supply, and the consumption of it, being the demand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This allows Singapore to retain all tools and levers to reduce the flow of drugs into Singapore and the abuse of drugs on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of this, will MDA be further bolstered to meet the morphing drug threat, for example, the new advertising of sale of drugs through the Internet, new psychoactive substances that enter the market every now and then, and more users making up new abusers?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As regards promotion and the principle of rehabilitation, would MHA consider quashing the drug consumption convictions or record for a former drug abuser who has kept away from drugs for several years, for example, two, three or five years?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This can be tracked from his regulated urine test.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such a quashing of his record will seriously incentivise him to stay clean for those number of years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The result is a win for himself, a win for his family, and a win for current drug inmates who have a real role model to follow.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Chairman, I visited the Community Rehabilitation Centre (CRC) recently.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is a community-based drug rehabilitation centre run by Trybe, a youth sector organisation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It houses male first-time drug abusers between the ages of 16 and 21.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: During the visit, I also learnt of the changing profile of drug abusers and drugs used in Singapore over the years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: At CRC, the approach taken is to immerse residents in a relationship-driven, transformational environment to lead a purposeful and drug-free life.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I am glad to know that we are taking a differentiated approach to help different drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Rehabilitation is one of the three key components in tackling the drug problems here, the other two being education and deterrence.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Other countries are increasingly taking a soft stance towards drugs, and liberal attitudes are seeping into our youths through social media and other channels.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: One of the residents at CRC shared that he was first introduced to drugs by the beach while on holiday.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is becoming more important that we set out our own narrative to counter inaccurate perceptions, to explain our approach and to show its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, as my colleague Mr Christopher de Souza has outlined earlier, the two most concerning statistics from the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) report in 2017 are: firstly, that the proportion of new drug abusers, even if the absolute numbers may have dropped slightly by proportion, as Mr de Souza said, 40% of drug abusers arrested are new abusers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Third, the common type of drug abuse, the methamphetamine, continues, by far, to be No 1 by about some distance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These numbers tell us that there is an increasing number of new abusers who are young, with a choice of drug being methamphetamine, which is fast gaining popularity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is a drug which is synthetically manufactured, which makes it easier to produce, and it is no coincidence that of worldwide seizures of drugs, methamphetamine constitutes the highest proportion, out of which the greatest volume seized come from East and Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Drug production facilities are known to be located near to Singapore, which places our country at a greater risk of having those drugs come onto our shores.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is a serious social cost arising from the breakup of families of addicts, the drop or lack of productivity, the cost of rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is also the problem caused by drug-related crimes, commonly stealing, housebreaking, robbery, all of which go towards supporting the habit, and they lend themselves to a less safe Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is clear that we must continue the vigilance and the absolute zero-tolerance policy against drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: To that end, can I ask the Minister to outline the steps taken to continue the fight against drug abuse?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, what additional steps can be taken to particularly focus on and educate potential new young abusers?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: What further strategies can be employed to make preventive drug education more effective not only to educate, but to proactively encourage and promote a drug-free lifestyle amongst the young?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, given the drug situation worsening regionally and worldwide, Singapore remains largely drug-free.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our drug abuse rate is very low, compared to other countries.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: CNB has been effective in their enforcement efforts and their fight against drugs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One of them is the use of drugs among the young.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is also a rise in online drug pedalling, with the number of people arrested for buying drugs online increasing over the last few years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most of those who engaged in online drug pedalling were between the ages of 20 and 39.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The change in mindset among the young, and the convenience offered by cyberspace, are perhaps important factors contributing to the rise in youth drug abuse.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My worry is that if such trends hold up, new young abusers may form the next generation of drug addicts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Once a youth is enslaved by drugs, it potentially means many years of hidden suffering for him and his loved ones.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask how MHA intends to better engage youths who are on drugs and tackle the high proportion of new young drug abusers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Given the preference and habits of our youths, does the Ministry intend to make use of the new and relevant engagement platforms, for example, social media, as part of its outreach?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have a soft spot for the families of those who are incarcerated for drug offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have close relatives who were incarcerated for drug-related offences and were in and out of prison for many years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I saw how their families were affected by this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Fortunately, the families overcame their challenges and the children are now all grown up, working and meaningfully contributing to the economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Not all families are as fortunate, as we have seen many cases where children of the drug offenders becoming addicts themselves.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is, therefore, important to continue to create awareness about the dangers and impact of drug abuse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is also important to support the families and ensure that there are proper rehabilitation and support upon release of the drug offenders from prison so that they can continue living their lives and participate in the future economy like everyone else.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Difficulties in getting a job or inability to have a stable income in a challenging economy can contribute towards these ex-offenders succumbing to temptations and reoffending.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The effort put in by the Ministry in the "Dadah itu Haram" campaign to tackle offending, reoffending and the drug abuse issue within the Malay/Muslim community is, therefore, commendable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I note that there is outreach to the Malay/Muslim organisations to help support this campaign.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What has been the community’s response to the campaign?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What is the status of the current efforts and further plans to work with the Malay/Muslim organisations in this regard?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take the three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: While the public’s support is important during reintegration, the ex-offender himself must be motivated to change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Inmates are the most disoriented, vulnerable and susceptible to influences at the initial incarceration phase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This would be the opportune time to render positive and aspirational elements, such as talks or programmes by successful ex-offenders, who can be role models for inmates during this initial phase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This would be a more powerful source of influence, compared to the counsel of case workers who may seem clinical and unrelatable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This would counter negative influences from fellow inmates discussing past escapades.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I recently had coffee with ex-offenders and the stories they shared with me were heartening and inspiring.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They made mistakes but they are trying hard to rebuild their lives and we need to help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If there is one word they used most frequently in their stories, it is "family".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I shared in my cuts last year, I strongly believe we should strengthen family ties to improve the rehabilitation process for inmates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am grateful that the Singapore Prison Service (SPS) is working with Focus on the Family Singapore on running programmes to strengthen family bonds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They were also not in their prison uniform.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the words of Focus on the Family Singapore "Humans thrive when we know we are loved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: When inmates connect and are reconciled with their families, there is a lower chance of them reoffending." Next, current in-care programmes for inmates feature psychological and cognitive-based curriculum and counselling, targeting the thinking and behavioural aspects of inmates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Programmes can come across as overly clinical, diagnostic, prescriptive, featuring lecture-style methods.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope the Ministry will consider featuring more inspirational, experiential and reflective learning approaches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For example, through mentoring, where community partners or representatives can come in regularly through group or one-on-one mentoring for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This could complement the "through-care" strategy of SPS, where the mentoring relationship could carry on into the Aftercare stages of the inmate, making societal reintegration more seamless.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This also provides a more humanistic approach targeting the heart of inmates, creating an authentic and positive relationship of trust.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, one of the best ways to help an ex-offender reintegrate into society is to help him secure and hold down a good job.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only will the job sustain him financially, it will also provide meaning to his life, enabling him to be a valued member of our community as he contributes his skills and expertise at work.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, matching jobs with ex-offenders is easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On one hand, the prisoners’ aptitude, attitude and interests have to be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, due to social stigma, employers have to overcome the psychological hurdle and take a leap of faith before giving an ex-offender an employment opportunity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The speed of change at our workplaces has become so rapid that even many of the gainfully employed are at risk of being left behind.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is why we have to constantly send our employees for training to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, imagine the knowledge and skills gap faced by ex-offenders after they are released from prison.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we cannot help them to bridge that gap, it would be difficult to bring down the rate of recidivism.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What types of learning programmes are available to prisoners and how does the Ministry encourage them to take up these courses?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the main challenges and obstacles faced by the prisoners and trainers?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our legislation seeks to help offenders find a path back into mainstream life in order to be active, contributing members of society, after they have spent their time in prison.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This helps because, upon reaching the five-year period, such offenders will be able to probably say that they do not have a further criminal conviction record.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the ex-offender is not able to find his place back in society, the prospect of his re-offending becomes much higher.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Would some of these steps include developing a strong after-care support network for the inmate and his or her family which, in fact, can be set up even during the period of incarceration in order to improve the prospects of successful reintegration?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, our Home Team has done an impeccable job in keeping us safe.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, it has its work cut out going ahead.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because of technology, crimes and social issues are fast-evolving, complex and multifaceted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Coupled with a leaner workforce, MHA must evolve new ways of staying ahead of the criminals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Home Team is undergoing an important transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Minister provide further updates on the Home Team’s transformation process, especially in improving coordination and interoperability across different agencies?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How has it resulted in more effective enforcement?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How have the community partnerships evolved to help in Home Team’s work?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And what will be the focus of the Home Team's outreach efforts in the coming year?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In MHA’s ongoing transformation, I hope that we can make an even greater shift towards tapping upon and empowering the individual and community entities in crime prevention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The fast-evolving, extraterritorial and multifaceted nature of crimes make purely Home Team-led actions more challenging over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we need to enhance capabilities to develop and test new ideas quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The fast-evolving nature of crimes and community issues meant no entity has the monopoly of good solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: MHA needs to develop platforms that will increase the academic and community participation in analysing and developing local solutions to our Home Team issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This might involve building up a national databank, such as Iceland’s Registers Iceland (ISCRA), where partners can use the data for analysis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is much like building on open-source codes where coders write and test new codes to build ever more robust systems quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, we can leverage even greater use of behavioural insights to tackle our youth drug addiction problems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The thrill for such young abusers is usually boredom and not getting caught.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are not always from traditionally defined broken homes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This means that while we cannot go soft on our tough stance against drugs, we must develop new ways of finding new solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Programmes, such as “Natural Highs” in Iceland, succeeded because of strong behavioural insights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could MHA similarly develop stronger behavioural insights in informing our future programmes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have worked hard at roadshows and awareness campaigns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, it is timely to make cyber health checks as commonplace as our basic health checks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a mindset shift that cyber issues similarly require routine and pervasive intervention as do chronic health problems, especially for older residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Community partners can work with the Home Team to develop easy to use diagnostic kits and help our elderly users stay healthier, cyberwise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Fourth, we can make greater use of integrated data analytics for predictive enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While crime-mapping is not new, the availability of artificial intelligence (AI) opens up new horizons in more effective manpower-lean policing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, this is not about going down the route of the movie “Minority Report”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is about better understanding our key threats and developing targeted effective solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Effective transformation also requires that our officers can take on the new jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Minister provide further updates on the job redesign efforts for the Home Team?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How many jobs or functions have been redesigned?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How has the Ministry also tapped on the expertise of retired officers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is important that we continue upskilling our private security workforce with better knowledge, better skills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But on my house visits, I have also met some older rank-and-file workers who want to join the security sector but find the courses unnecessarily complicated.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They have found that some training materials are very wordy and not written in simple English.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One Clementi resident I met on my house visits was very discouraged.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He speaks well, communicates easily and has lots of energy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But because he only went to primary school 50 years ago, his reading and writing in English are not so strong.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He showed me a page from the training handbook.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I saw the page and I ran the text through Microsoft Word which can calculate how hard it is to read the text.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Microsoft Word said that the reading difficulty is like an American senior high-school or university level grade.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As comparison, one American President's State of the Union speech from the 1980s had an easier reading level than that page from the training handbook!

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, my residents and people like him – they are good men and women – they did not choose to be born in a time when primary school education was the best opportunity that they had.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many of my older residents still have much to contribute.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They are able-bodied, can communicate with the public without difficulty, keen to learn, but for people like my residents, they are finding it difficult to get into the private security industry, even though an opportunity there can provide much-needed income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Security threats to common installations and public spaces in Singapore are very real concerns.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, the security industry is facing a serious manpower crunch.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst technology and new advances in security devices, drones and the like can help plug the gap, there remains a need for well-qualified and experienced security consultants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The IPA requires the submission of security plans for approval to the commissioner and, subsequently, the implementation of the measures in the plan after approval.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The plan is the foundation of an enhanced protection of special developments and infrastructure under IPA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is, therefore, critical that there are sufficient, well-qualified and recognised professionals who can come up with and implement robust and well-considered security plans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Taking a leaf out of my colleague Dr Tan Wu Meng who spoke earlier, could there be more options for persons who are otherwise interested in this industry but find that the bar to entry to the industry is too high, for reasons Dr Tan cited?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Could the Minister also consider other types of qualifications, aside from having just the specialist diploma, including certifications from professional bodies, university degrees in security and other qualifications, which are very much practical in nature on the ground, and from people who have vast experience, because security is one industry where leaving aside the books, leaving aside the difficulty in language, experience counts for a lot more than what one might read from the textbooks?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Public trust and confidence in the Home Team continue to be high.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The overall crime and drug situation remains under control.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the number of drug abusers arrested decreased in 2017, compared to 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fire incidents are at their lowest in 40 years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Recidivism rates have improved, as have the road safety and immigration offending situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the overall situation in 2017 on the security front was, I would say, better than previous years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And compared to the rest of the world, many other similar cities, we are in a good situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Achieving those results, securing a safer Singapore requires efforts from many different people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We look at the growing terrorism threat, we have to deal with it on multiple fronts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also means building up our capabilities to protect our people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A large part of that increase is going into enhancing our counterterrorism capabilities and efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is because the threat of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) remains high and, in fact, will continue to grow, as fighters from the Middle East come back to this region.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MHA must and will do all it can to protect our people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is our responsibility and accountability to deal with terrorist threats within Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Members may know, under our system, legal framework and constitutional structure, MHA is responsible for home-front and internal security, including counterterrorism, crisis and consequence management.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When a terrorist attack happens, MHA is, therefore, overall responsible, will be in charge and lead the national response.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Police will manage the incidents on the ground and will be the first and main responders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the scale of the attack is very large, MHA may also ask SAF to provide support to the Police as an auxiliary force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Likewise, MHA may also ask other Ministries, agencies, like the Ministry of Health (MOH) to support the operations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To this end, the Police and SAF have developed joint plans and conducted joint exercises.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are, of course, very appreciative for the SAF's commitment and the commitment of other agencies to support the Home Team in such situations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This modus operandi has been discussed and agreed on for some time and, as I have said, it follows the constitutional structure and practice that we have adopted over many decades and I made this clear in 2016, when I stated that all operations within Singapore, the Police will take command.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And depending on the nature and the scale of the attack, Home Team may rely on other agencies which will provide support for us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These agencies could include, depending on the nature and scale of the incident, SAF, the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) and MOH.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, if there is a large-scale attack, if Police need additional forces beyond the Emergency Response Teams (ERT) and the Special Operations Command (SOC), SPF may call upon SAF for specialised forces like the Special Operations Task Force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will also support and reinforce the ERTs and SOC.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Exercises have been conducted to make sure that these plans are sharpened and we will continue to include other partner agencies in such exercises.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second Minister Josephine Teo will share more on how the Home Team is countering the terrorist threat.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, ensuring the criminal justice system stays relevant and effective; second, preventing religious extremism and segregationist thinking; and third, maintaining our tough stance against drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The other officeholders will deal with the other points.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We seek to amend the CPC, the Bill that is in Parliament – the Evidence Act – and later this year, we will amend the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The detailed proposals on the amendments to CPC will be covered in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I told the House in January that we have embarked on a comprehensive review of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We set up a committee in July 2016 to this end to undertake a fundamental review to look at the principles which underlie our laws, what offences could be covered, what the punishments should be, and whether the current punishments are appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Committee aims to complete its work in a few months' time, and we will invite feedback from the public.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Significant focus of the Penal Code Review would be on enhancing protections for vulnerable persons – children, people with mental disabilities and domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have seen cases where such persons are violently treated, hurt, exploited or even killed by the very people who ought to be protecting them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many Members will know of the case of Annie Ee, as do many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We can understand the anger that many people felt.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Recently, the case of a mother who abused her two-year-old son.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And after two years, he died from head injuries, assaulted for not being able to recite numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our punishments for these sorts of offences are generally stiff.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will, nevertheless, review the punishments and what is the level of proof that is needed for these cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng spoke about the Vulnerable Adults Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our MSF colleagues have been working hard on this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I understand the Bill will be tabled in Parliament soon.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, I want to talk about process reviews and changes, the steps we are taking to improve our processes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you look at investigations, our investigative processes, will aim to take better care of the victims' well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In particular, we are looking at the investigations and Court processes for sexual crimes, to better protect victims of such offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Louis Ng asked about this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I first announced in August 2016 that we were reviewing this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have listened to the victims to understand their concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have worked with several organisations – MSF, hospitals, Courts and non-government organisations (NGOs) – to improve our processes and the way our officers interact with the victims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Victims can be examined by a doctor onsite at the Criminal Investigation Department (CID), without the need to shuttle between CID and hospital and having to recount what happened to them once at the hospital and once to the Police Officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Everything could be done in one place, at the OneSAFE Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have developed a training video for our officers on how to question the victims in an empathetic way.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) helped us with that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will then understand and have greater empathy for the trauma faced by victims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This would be focused on children who have been sexually abused by family members.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is necessary to gather the facts from these children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, again, one can imagine or understand the stress that such children may undergo if they have to be interviewed separately by the Police, doctors and child protection officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so, we will seek to integrate these interviews so that the children need not repeatedly recount their traumatic experience.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In addition, Court processes will aim to better protect the victims of sexual assault cases, including automatic protection of identity, closed-door hearings and the questions about the victim's sexual history and unrelated behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be restrictions on what sort of cross-examination will be allowed, subject to the overall jurisdiction of the Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will be set out when we deal with the legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will define the precise scope, what we are intending to do, and how the process can be taken forward.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another process is the Appropriate Adults (AAs) Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We started this in 2013 for persons with intellectual disabilities and mental health problems.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was extended in 2017 to support young suspects.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are trained to provide emotional support to the interviewees.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2017, AAs provided support for about 700 interviews during the course of investigations, and the feedback has been positive, both from the volunteers who are AAs, as well as the Investigation Officers (IOs).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In April this year, we will roll out the AA scheme to more Police and CNB units so that they can support more young suspects.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And it will also include Customs and the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Separately, we are also looking to identify and deal with the basic issues that lead people to crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke about involving the community and VWOs, and how to deal with offenders with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When our officers deal with individuals who have committed offences, often, they become aware of other problems and the complex circumstances surrounding these offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Mr Murali Pillai pointed out, some have medical issues, too.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we will have these CARES officers stationed at every Police Division.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The CARES officers will assess whether social interventions are needed to address the underlying issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The interventions could be in the form of counselling; it could be in the form of mental health assistance; it could be in the form of financial assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The CARES officers will then refer the offenders to a suitable agency for help and continue to follow-up.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are studying this in detail with MSF, and we will try to pilot this at a Police Division this year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another important area is how we deal with the young offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach, if you take today, 80% of the youths who are arrested are not charged – four out of five are not charged.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police will give them a warning and refer them to counselling and other programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to give them a chance to sober up, stay on the right side of the law after that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there will be cases, as the statistics showed – 20% – where we have no choice.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some are repeat offenders; some could be serious offences, like drug trafficking.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And for punishment, deterrence and, equally important, their own rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Reformative Training (RT) is an essential, necessary regime for such young people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Within the RT population, we try to group them by risk profile and needs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This helps to provide a more targeted set of interventions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The trainees will go through programmes that will help them take charge of their rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can then reflect on their offences ‒ how to stay crime-free and how to strengthen their relationships with their family.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prisons will also continue with their education and skills training for the reformative trainees.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those who can, will continue to take their GCE "N", "O" and "A" levels.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are also vocational training opportunities, such as Workforce Development Agency (WDA)-accredited courses.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We intend to further enhance the RT regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is in line with the more targeted approach we want to take because different individuals may require different intensities of intervention and different lengths of rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will speak further about the RT regime during the Second Reading of the CPC (Amendment) Bill later this month.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My third point, let me deal with religious extremism and segregationist thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The older generation, who are getting increasingly older, will remember the turmoil of the 1950s and 1960s.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not want to go back to those days.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For many countries, that is their current reality.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What we have today is the racial and religious harmony which has been achieved through decades of deliberate and sustained intervention and the Government working hand-in-hand with various stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We never say you have arrived, and you can slide back quite quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, how do we prevent segregationist teachings from taking root?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have a number of approaches – social intervention, regulatory framework and a constant working with community organisations, grassroots, getting the message across.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, in terms of social intervention, our Ethnic Integration Policy in our public housing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: National Service (NS) puts our young men together.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These deliberate interventions mean that we grow up together, build collective memories together and we come together as Singaporeans, instead of forming ethnic or religious enclaves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And this shows in the way we live our daily lives, such as eating together at the same table, working together in the same offices.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One example of the approach or the result of that approach, the Straits Times recently featured Masjid Khalid, a mosque in Joo Chiat, which distributes oranges and greeting cards to business owners and residents in the area during the Lunar New Year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is just one of the many examples we see on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to preserve the harmony and, to do this, we cannot let extremist or segregationist teachings infiltrate our communities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even a small number of persons propagating radical, segregationist beliefs can be dangerous.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Mr Chong Kee Hiong pointed out, the inflammatory and viral potential of such beliefs is increased with social media.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we work closely with community groups and religious organisations, we want to try and better inoculate our community from such influences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the efforts extend to online as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, the Religious Rehabilitation Group (RRG) has produced online videos to explain why ISIS' ideology goes against Islamic teachings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Offline, in the physical world, when we have foreign preachers who want to come into Singapore, and if we know that they have advocated violence or spread ill-will towards other religions, whether in Singapore or elsewhere, they will not be allowed to speak here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One of them had described Allah as "a false god".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He had asked for prayers for those "held captive in the darkness of Islam".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He insinuated that Buddhists were "lost" people who could be saved by converting to Christianity.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The other preacher had variously referred to "the malevolent nature of Islam and Mohammed", saying Islam was "not a religion of peace".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we said no, they cannot come in to preach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They wanted to come into Singapore to preach on a religious-themed cruise.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is wrong with Mufti Menk telling Muslims that wishing non-Muslims "Merry Christmas" or "Happy Deepavali" is the biggest sin and crime that a Muslim can commit?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mufti Menk is a preacher who has been systematically putting out messages like there are people who are very big enemies of Islam, and if you attend their functions, you will be seen as rubbing shoulders with them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are thousands of reasons why Islam is more authentic and valuable; that Christianity is just a bubble that is blown such that you feel emotionally high.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at all his teachings, the main message that comes out is quite clear and the divisiveness is not acceptable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, we are also not immune to Islamophobia.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So far, these incidents are few and far between.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is because of the approach of the Government and the people of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we need to keep a close watch on this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We must not allow the threat of terrorism to, on the other side, create fear, suspicion and distrust of one another.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong spoke about the role of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our community leaders have done much to foster respect and understanding among the communities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs) are one example.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our religious leaders play a big role in leading by example.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A wonderful example is the Mufti of Singapore, Dr Mohamed Fatris Bakaram, who shares in other communities' celebrations like Deepavali and Christmas, and regularly offers festive greetings in private and public, including during the Chinese New Year last month.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another example is the Anglican Bishop Rennis Ponniah who hosted an annual Christmas tea at his official residence, with not just Anglicans attending, but also Catholics, Lutherans, Muslims, Buddhists and Taoists.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were invited to join in and they joined it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Singapore Buddhist Lodge donates rice and funds to mosques during Ramadan every year for the breaking of fast, to be distributed to needy families.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was initiated by their late President Mr Lee Bock Guan, both to help the needy and to promote inter-religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is the respect of different faiths, the willingness to share in one another's lives, that it is not just a harmonious common living space.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Baey Yam Keng, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Edwin Tong spoke about the global challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to stay firm in this fight against drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are also studying how we can enhance the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) to deal with new threats.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the past year, the drug situation in the world has continued to worsen.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The US declared the opioid crisis they face is a "public health emergency".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sixty-four thousand people – that number is more than the number of US soldiers who died in the Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq wars combined.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is more than the number of people who have died through breast cancer in the US.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is more than the number of people who have died of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-related deaths in the US at the peak of the epidemic.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The media has covered extensively on how the big pharmaceutical (pharma) companies, poor regulation and irresponsible proliferation of poor-quality research often funded by the pharma companies have all combined to create this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In May 2017, the US federal court found top executives from Purdue Pharma guilty of misleading regulators, doctors, patients about the risks of OxyContin, which is a powerful and addictive opioid.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Patients graduated from snorting or injecting the crushed pills, then turning to heroin and other drugs to feed their addictions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Despite the harms caused by drugs, some countries have been softening their stance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Countries, such as Portugal, have decriminalised drug use and they have received international attention for this approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And there are some people here who tell us Portugal is a great example to follow and show why our approach is wrong and Portugal's approach is right.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And what are the lessons for us from the Portugal situation?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, Portugal started with a serious public health problem on its hands.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were sharing contaminated needles and they were spreading diseases like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C and HIV.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: More than half of the HIV infections were drug-related, which was the highest rate in the European Union (EU).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It increased funding for treatment facilities, provided for needle exchange and opioid substitution therapy, ran campaigns "say no to a second-hand syringe".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These measures have helped Portugal to reduce HIV and Hepatitis infections.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But when you start with serious HIV-related problems, Hepatitis infection-related problems arising through drug use, contaminated needles, then I suppose you ask yourself which is the lesser evil and you go for decriminalisation and then you try and reduce the problem somewhat.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we are not in that situation, thankfully.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Surveys indicate that more Portuguese students are trying drugs and the number of drug-related deaths has also gone up since 2011.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you will not find all these facts from the people who advocate that we go down the route of Portugal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Portugal decided to decriminalise drugs in a situation where perhaps it concluded that it was not possible or unrealistic for it to control the drug situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The situation we have in Singapore is different.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach has been effective and has worked well for us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are one of the few countries where the drug situation has been under control and perhaps the country that has been most effective in dealing with the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, can I display a slide on the screen, please?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have many slides, but this sort of shows you what the trends have been over a period of time in terms of drug use.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anyway, in all the downward blip for the period when people abused Subutex, when you see that, it is probably a fairly smooth curve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was not a real dip in certain years because people were using Subutex.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then we outlawed that and they went back to other drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of drug abusers we have in Singapore is relatively low, compared with some of the other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Portugal, it is just under 20 times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the numbers will grow further in the US because of the move towards legalisation in many states.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you take that as 3,000 to 4,000 lives per year over a 20-year period, it is a lot of lives, a lot of people who have been saved from drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This result has been possible because we have been tough on drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just this Monday, CNB arrested a trafficker in a drug bust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the investigations, officers discovered that ‒ and it was a lady ‒ she was caregiver to a toddler.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She had left him with two other suspected drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Concerned about the toddler's safety, CNB and Police then moved quickly with operations the very next day to take down two suspects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The young child was rescued and is now with Child Protective Services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that one year, the young child had already been abandoned by his mother, who is on the run for drug offences, and being passed around between drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In many other countries, these are par for the course.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In another case, a drug addict father abused his baby daughter ‒ very cruel, regularly biting her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One day, he was furious because he had no money to buy drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The baby cried ‒ as babies do ‒ and he shoved her against the wall so hard, her skull fractured.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She was 10 months old ‒ not old enough to defend herself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The activists light candles for traffickers outside Changi Prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But who cares for these very real victims?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How many young lives have we saved with our policies?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would you hear a squeak from the activists about these people ‒ the actual victims of burglaries, housebreakings, families torn apart through drugs, the physical violence, the mental abuse, and, by a process of estimation, the number of people who have been saved from that, the shootings and the killings that take place in other countries where drug abuse is prevalent?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The 60,000 people who died through opioid abuse do not capture all the deaths in the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many more gangland violence with drugs as the underlying cause ‒ the shootings, guns, weapons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have another case in Singapore – a 9-year-old boy living with his abusive aunt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He ran away because he was scared of being beaten again when she was under the influence of drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But she found him, hit him, burned him with a lighter, picked him up and dangled him out of a third-storey window.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our CNB officers recently came across another abuser – seven months pregnant, still smoking "ice".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She already had a previous miscarriage because of her "ice" habit, but her addiction was so strong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She persisted anyway, at the expense of her unborn, innocent child.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, again, from foreign jurisdictions, you see cases where children are born with addiction in-built and they need and crave for heroin from the time they are born.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said earlier, the self-styled activists refused to talk about how the addiction of hundreds of abusers is fed with each shipment that these traffickers bring in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How many families suffer as a result of drugs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our penalties are severe because we want to deter such offences, not because we take any joy in enforcing them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one can take any joy in enforcing them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The region is home to the Golden Triangle, which is the largest methamphetamine market in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Being a major transport and commercial hub makes us susceptible, both as a transit point and as an import market because of the wealth factor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is beyond our ability to change factors outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we can do is to try and deter criminals from attempting to bring drugs into Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have to be firm in resisting those who try to force their ideologies on us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin will elaborate on how we are working with various stakeholders on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Chairman, there were some 20 minutes of savings from the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In order for Parliamentary Secretary Amrin and I to address the remaining cuts, may we have your kind consent to take that extra time?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members spoke about the different challenges that the Home Team faces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will expand on MHA's responses in three areas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, counterterrorism; second, Home Team transformation, and that is not just in technology but also in manpower; and third, on the private security industry.
